match.reason: None of the bank points teach arc length of a parametric curve or the surface area of a solid of revolution by integration; the closest, arcs and sectors, covers only circular arc length with rθ at Year 11 depth, and the others cover signed area, area between curves, scaling, and prism surface area.

draft.title: Arc length and surface area
card: A curve given by x = x(t) and y = y(t), for a ≤ t ≤ b, has length L = ∫ √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt, from t = a to t = b. The root comes from Pythagoras on a tiny piece of the curve.
If the curve is y = f(x), use L = ∫ √(1 + (dy/dx)²) dx, from x = a to x = b.
Rotating the curve y = f(x) about the x-axis makes a surface. Its area is S = 2π ∫ y √(1 + (dy/dx)²) dx. Each tiny piece of length is spun around a circle of circumference 2πy.
Example: x = t², y = 2t for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1 gives dx/dt = 2t and dy/dt = 2. So L = ∫ √(4t² + 4) dt = 2∫ √(t² + 1) dt, from t = 0 to t = 1.
draft.remember: Length adds up tiny pieces √(dx² + dy²). Surface area multiplies each piece by 2πy.

a.q: A curve has x = 3t and y = 4t for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2. Using the arc length formula, what is its length?
a.why: dx/dt = 3 and dy/dt = 4, so the integrand is √(9 + 16) = 5. Then L = 5 × 2 = 10. Answer 5 forgets to integrate over the interval of length 2.
a.clue: The integrand is constant, so multiply it by the length of the t interval.

b.q: The line y = 2x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 is rotated about the x-axis. What is the surface area, using S = 2π ∫ y √(1 + (dy/dx)²) dx?
b.why: dy/dx = 2, so √(1 + 4) = √5. Then S = 2π ∫ 2x√5 dx = 2π√5 × [x²] from 0 to 1 = 2π√5. Answer 4π√5 forgets that the integral of 2x is x², not 2x². Answer 4π leaves out the √5 factor.
b.clue: Put y = 2x into the integrand, and keep the factor √(1 + (dy/dx)²).

check.summary: No problems found. The formulas, the worked example and both intended answers (10 and 2π√5, which matches the cone lateral area πrl = π·2·√5) are correct.

final.title: Arc length and surface area
card: A curve given by \(x = x(t)\) and \(y = y(t)\), for \(a \le t \le b\), has length \(L = \int \sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^{2}} \, dt\), from \(t = a\) to \(t = b\). The root comes from Pythagoras on a tiny piece of the curve.
If the curve is \(y = f(x)\), use \(L = \int \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}} \, dx\), from \(x = a\) to \(x = b\).

Rotating the curve \(y = f(x)\) about the x-axis makes a surface. Its area is \(S = 2\pi \int y \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}} \, dx\). Each tiny piece of length is spun around a circle of circumference \(2\pi y\).

Example: \(x = t^{2}\), \(y = 2t\) for \(0 \le t \le 1\) gives \(\frac{dx}{dt} = 2t\) and \(\frac{dy}{dt} = 2\). So \(L = \int \sqrt{4t^{2} + 4} \, dt = 2\int \sqrt{t^{2} + 1} \, dt\), from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 1\).
final.remember: Length adds up tiny pieces \(\sqrt{(dx)^{2} + (dy)^{2}}\). Surface area multiplies each piece by \(2\pi y\).

a.q: A curve has \(x = 3t\) and \(y = 4t\) for \(0 \le t \le 2\). Using the arc length formula, what is its length?
a.why: \(\frac{dx}{dt} = 3\) and \(\frac{dy}{dt} = 4\), so the integrand is \(\sqrt{9 + 16} = 5\). Then \(L = 5 \times 2 = 10\). Answer 5 forgets to integrate over the interval of length 2.
a.clue: The integrand is constant, so multiply it by the length of the \(t\) interval.

b.q: The line \(y = 2x\) for \(0 \le x \le 1\) is rotated about the x-axis. What is the surface area, using \(S = 2\pi \int y \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}} \, dx\)?
b.why: \(\frac{dy}{dx} = 2\), so \(\sqrt{1 + 4} = \sqrt{5}\). Then \(S = 2\pi \int_{0}^{1} 2x\sqrt{5} \, dx\), which is \(2\pi\sqrt{5} \times \left[x^{2}\right]_{0}^{1} = 2\pi\sqrt{5}\). Answer \(4\pi\sqrt{5}\) forgets that the integral of \(2x\) is \(x^{2}\), not \(2x^{2}\). Answer \(2\pi\) leaves out the \(\sqrt{5}\) factor.
b.clue: Put \(y = 2x\) into the integrand, and keep the factor \(\sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}}\).
